To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the experience of abstinence and relapse in alcohol-dependent patients is associated with changes in alcohol-related risk perception, and (2) these changes are associated with abstinence during the 12-month follow-up.

(1) alcohol-related risk perception changes during alcohol use disorder treatment, (2), changes vary with treatment related experiences of abstinence and relapse indicating “risk reappraisal”, (3) adjustment to perceived own vulnerability according the “risk reapprraisal hypothesis” predicts abstinence during treatment.

the risk perception of patients with alcohol use disorder changes in response to treatment experiences and that the change of risk perception during treatment is predictive of abstinence during follow up.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether and under what circumstances the risk perception of alcohol-dependent persons is susceptible to change and whether changes in risk perception are linked to alcohol consumption.
the relationship between alcohol use and alcohol-related risk perception.
the role of risk perception for treatment success in AUD patients and its underlying mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present study show an impact of experience-induced change of risk perception on alcohol use in AUD treatment.
alcohol-related risk perception is not a stable trait, but rather an experience-dependent state variable that is related to treatment outcome.
the results of this study are in line with the risk reappraisal hypothesis, and therefore, it is recommended to integrate the risk reappraisel hypothesis into AUD treatments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alcohol-related risk perception changes during alcohol use disorder treatment, and these changes may have an impact on alcohol use during the follow-up.
the more a patient perceives himself at risk for relapse, the better his treatment outcome is.

the experience of abstinence and relapse during AUD treatment leads to changes in the perception of one’s own alcohol-related risks, and that the extent to which this risk reappraisal occurs predicts abstinence during the 12 months after treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
alcohol-related risk perception changes in the course of AUD treatment.
risk appraisal is not a static construct, but can be modified by experiences, such as abstinence and relapse.
alcohol-related risk perception changes in a treatment context and that the change in perceived own vulnerability is associated with abstinence.
